questions.q: Per this lesson's six-step process, what should come first when starting a glossary?
options: Pick one scoped domain, rather than the whole organization at once
Buy the most expensive glossary software available
Delete all existing documentation before starting
Define every possible business term in the organization simultaneously
questions.explain: A glossary for one domain, done well, is more valuable than a half-finished glossary attempting all domains at once — the same scoped-pilot logic from Data Governance Foundations.

questions.q: According to this lesson, which terms should a new glossary effort list first?
options: Every term that could theoretically ever be defined, in alphabetical order
The terms people actually argue about or define differently today
Only terms that are already perfectly defined elsewhere
Terms chosen at random from the database schema
questions.explain: Starting with real, current points of confusion delivers value faster than exhaustively cataloging every possible term up front.

questions.q: In the worked Customer-domain mini-glossary, what is the relationship between 'Client' and 'Customer'?
options: 'Client' is deprecated and marked as a synonym pointing to 'Customer'
They are unrelated, competing terms with separate definitions
'Client' is the parent term and 'Customer' is its child
'Client' replaced 'Customer' as the new official term
questions.explain: The worked example marks 'Client' as deprecated, with its entry pointing back to 'Customer' as the one official term — exactly the synonym pattern from Lesson 9.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a common early-stage mistake when building a glossary?
options: Skipping the approval step 'just this once' to move faster
Scoping the first effort to a single domain
Reviewing definitions with people outside the project team
Modeling relationships between related terms
questions.explain: The lesson warns that the first unapproved term that turns out wrong is the one that costs the whole glossary its credibility — skipping approval even once is risky.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a glossary must be 'published and announced,' not just built?
options: Because a glossary nobody knows exists provides zero value — this is the metadata lifecycle's publish stage
Because publishing is a legal requirement in every country
Because unpublished glossaries automatically delete themselves after 30 days
Because only published glossaries can contain more than ten terms
questions.explain: This connects back to the metadata lifecycle from Lesson 4 — publish is as easy to skip as maintain, and a hidden glossary delivers no actual value.
